newsitem.title: MEXICO: Latam group wins prize for sheltering street kids.
newsitem.headline: Latam group wins prize for sheltering street kids.

text.p: Briton Bruce Harris has been shot at and publicly criticised for his work in support of Latin American street children, but on Tuesday he set out to receive a prestigious award for his efforts.

Casa Alianza, an orphanage run by Harris in Mexico and Central America with the support of the British-based Covenant House, has won the Olof Palme Award, named after the slain Swedish prime minister and handed out by his family.
Harris, also singled out as an individual winner of the award, left Mexico City on Tuesday with three street children to get the prize and a check for $38,000 in Sweden on Thursday.

This is the 10th annual Olof Palme award and the first given to a Latin American organisation. Jose Manuel Capellin, the executive director for Casa Alianza in Mexico, called it "the equivalent of the Nobel prize."

"Olof Palme was internationally renowned for his work on the side of the downtrodden," Harris said at an airport news conference. "This is an opportunity to tell the world about the plight of street children and hopefully motivate people to do something about it."

Harris came to Mexico City three years ago to help Casa Alianza and the 13,000 children who live on the streets. The group gives children a new start, guiding them through a step-by-step programme that eventually leads to school or a job.

Before coming to Mexico, Harris brought international attention to the plight of street children in Guatemala who were being systematically murdered by shadowy groups sometimes linked to security forces.
Harris and his family were forced to leave when three armed men shot up his home in the middle of the night.

The problem of street children continues in Guatemala. Five of them between the ages of 12 and 14 have had their throats slit in the past eight weeks, he said, although the motive may have been simple crime.

In Honduras, Casa Alianza has denounced the cases of children locked up in adult jails, sometimes sharing cells with hardened criminals. The campaign was so vocal that Honduran Deputy Justice Minister Gladys Caballero last week accused Casa Alianza of "making a scandal" just to win awards.
"I know we're a pain in the neck sometimes," Harris said. "But all we're trying to do is improve the situation for the children."
